You wanted to have some meat for your family, for yourself. You've got a cow, you've got an animal, cut out a piece of the flesh of that animal, let the animal scam away, heal itself, scabs. You had another meal, and other meals. Well, this sensibility, this Jewish sensibility of compassion for feeling creatures, is, it seems to me, one of the underlying, and for me, the most persuasive aspect of keeping kosher. I am very taken by, for example, the vegetarian movement, which has, to my mind, many Jewish roots. We know, for example, that in Genesis, the human beings were told to eat of all of the vegetables or the fruits. And the assumption there was that you were not to be carnivorous, you would not be eating meats. And it was only after the flood where God makes a kind of concession to the animatic, carniviral aspects of man and says, "Okay, you can do it, but..." And then you have all these butts which says, "Make sure that you drain the blood." There's a kind of recognition that, ideally, this is not the way one should live. In addition to which, historically, we know that keeping kosher became one of the identifying marks of Jewishness. So that the Greek Syrians, that story which we tell around Hanukkah time, in order to break the national people, who will the people, forced swine down the throat of those people. So that became, even for non-religious Jews, a mark of pride and of dignity, not to eat, pig, etc., etc. My father, who was not a religious man, understood this, and that would be taboo. And the taboo was because of a respect for peoplehood and also the recognition that it somehow rather allows Jews to assemble together, so that my grandfather could feel freer to eat in our home, because he knew the home was. But that's part of it. But I do think that this vegetarian thing is more interesting that we've made of it. We have a vegetarian group here that meets at Valley Betscholom. And when we speak about it, a lot of things that motivate them is health, but a lot of things are ethics. It's interesting I mentioned the fact that, originally, the ingenesis, you have a vegetarian proclivity, but also in the messianic era, when you speak about the lion and lamb dwelling together, the assumption is, the picture is that it's a bivorous society, that everybody's going to eat vegetation. Because there's something intrinsically repulsive about the taking of a life of a living-feeling creature. I think my mind that his explanation is very meaningful to me. When he tries to explain the details of Kashrut in the Guide to the Perplexed, he constantly refers to the struggle against paganism, and a particular sabbienism. What he's saying is that, for example, in a milk, not cooking the milk, the kid in the mother's milk, is a protest against a sabbien-right, a religious pagan-right in which they did that. I think that historically there's an awful lot of mystery behind it, the rationale, originally, whether it could be done, even a question of the interpretation of what it means. Does it really say, "Lotivacheo gedibhehalevemo," you are not to cook a kid in his mother's milk, is it halav, or is it halav, is it milk, or is it fat? Because it is much as the Torah does not have diacritical marks, it's all consonants, you could read it the various way. My own feeling is that that is fascinating and interesting, that most important is not the genesis of a law, but what it became, historically. And it seems to me, as you've pointed out, that honey has been accepted as representation, and maybe the very notion of sweet that comes out of something that's not sweet is a kind of an orgery for what can happen, that nothing is irredeemable, that you can make something pure and noble, out of an origin that is less pure. I want to make one or a point of view, don't mind on this question of, you know, Jews, while they did not eat these prohibited food, like from mannebels, such as the pig. It's interesting that in Zoroastrianism, a religion which Jews experienced when they were exiled in Babylonia, there were two gods, a god of light and a god of darkness, and a struggle between both of them, and that the god of darkness was represented by these bad beasts, which you were then, if you were on the good side, killed. Never do you find, in Judaism, anything against those unco-shar animals, other than eating them. But you never go out to say, there's something evil in those animals, kill a pig, or kill a camel, nothing other. I think that's important. But the animals are created by God, and is thus touched by something of the divine hand. So, while historically these things develop, I think there is a deeper rationale to Kashrut, and I like to see what did Kashrut become, rather than what is the origin of it.

Historical conditions such as lack of refrigeration influenced early practices related to meat consumption.

Textual ambiguity in Hebrew script justifies interpretive flexibility in religious law.
The idea that purity can arise from impure origins supports a broader spiritual worldview.
Animals are not inherently evil; their moral status is independent of religious symbolism.

Now it seems to me that we have an opportunity, and we know from historians like Sélle Buran, that in Roman times you had easily 10% of the population, pagan population, which were Jewish. And the only reason we stopped proselytizing was that after Constantine and after the other emperors of Rome adopted Christianity as the established religion, they said if you convert a pagan to Judaism, then that Jew would risk capital punishment. Well that's enough to discourage it. But we're not living in Roman times. We're living in a free, democratic, pluralistic society, and we have to take advantage of it and return to the roots of Judaism, which said you ought to be enlightened to the nations. All predictions in the Jewish prophetic tradition are conditioned on the term 'if'.
The character of the speaker’s congregation improved positively after increasing outreach to converts.
Many Gentiles attending open sessions are seeking spiritual truth, not marrying into Jewish families.
There are approximately 13 to 14 million Jews worldwide today.
Gentiles often do not feel welcome in synagogues despite being spiritually curious.
Demographers and sociologists report interest in Judaism among people in Nigeria and India.
The 13th benediction of the Amida prayer includes praise for righteous Jews by choice.
People in Nigeria and India are drawn to Judaism due to its age, non-dogmatism, practicality, warmth, and family orientation.

assumptions.text: Spiritual seekers are worthy of genuine engagement regardless of their origin or background.
The moral foundation of Judaism rests on compassion for the marginalized, particularly strangers and converts.
Judaism’s authenticity is measured by its inclusivity toward outsiders and seekers.
Judaism’s mission historically included enlightening the nations, not isolating them.
Modern democratic societies provide safe conditions for renewed outreach and conversion efforts.
Abraham’s status as a pagan before becoming a Jew exemplifies the legitimacy of conversion.
The historical cessation of proselytization under Roman rule was due to state-enforced persecution, not theological rejection.
Outreach programs that foster mentorship deepen communal understanding and vitality.
Conversion should not be motivated by demographic replacement or fear of decline.
The term 'shiksa' and related derogatory terms reflect a deviation from authentic Jewish values.
